Trump Swaps Out Tariffs for Even More Tariffs. Foreign leaders accuse the White House of using forced labor allegations as a smokescreen for protectionist measures.

UK outlaws support for IRGC under new national security powers. Britain formally designated Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a threat to national security on Friday, making public support for the organization or assistance to it punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Iran’s rial hits new low as dollar nears 1.92 million. The US dollar reached a record 1,918,000 rials on Iran’s open market Friday, surpassing its previous high as war, inflation and worsening economic prospects continued to weaken the currency.

Iran hardliners blamed as cost of US strikes mounts. Moderate voices in Iran are sharpening their criticism of hardline calls for continued confrontation with the United States, arguing that diplomacy has become a patriotic necessity as renewed war exacts mounting economic and human costs.

US backs Iraq pipeline plans to bypass Hormuz. US-backed plans to revive an oil pipeline linking Iraq and Syria have gained new urgency as Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on shipping disrupt regional exports and drive oil prices higher.

Tehran demands media limit strike damage coverage as US widens war. A confidential directive from Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, obtained by Iran International on Friday, instructed media publishers and editors to limit reporting on damage to civilian infrastructure as the United States reportedly prepares to widen the Iran war.

Why US strikes are moving deeper into southern Iran. The latest US strikes on southern Iran may offer the clearest indication yet of how Washington's campaign around the Strait of Hormuz is evolving from retaliation to the systematic degradation of Iran's military infrastructure.

US strikes cut roads and bridges in southern Iran as ground assault talk grows. US strikes have destroyed bridges, tunnels and rail links across southern Iran in a seventh straight night of attacks, severing roads to the Strait of Hormuz coast and feeding talk in Washington and Tehran that a ground assault may follow.

New US troop deaths, Iran’s MoU suspension push war into darker phase. The deaths of two US service members in Iranian attacks on Jordan, Tehran’s suspension of its commitments under the memorandum with Washington and a new threat from Iran’s Supreme Leader have raised fears that the war is entering a darker and more dangerous phase.

Rubio signals diplomacy as US-Iran war escalates. The United States intensified its military campaign against Iran after the first confirmed American combat deaths of the conflict, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted Washington remained open to diplomacy with Tehran.

Iranian women being shut out of engineering fields, official warns. Women dominate Iran’s universities but remain sharply underrepresented in engineering and other technical fields, Iran’s vice president for women’s affairs said on Monday, calling for a review of admissions and the social barriers shaping their choices.

Pahlavi backs US-led war as ‘necessary’ to prevent further bloodshed in Iran. Iran’s exiled prince Reza Pahlavi said in an interview with Reuters that the US-led war against the Islamic Republic was a “necessary step” to prevent further bloodshed and give Iranians a better chance of ending clerical rule.

Family of executed protester says he was tortured into false confession. The family of 37-year-old executed protester Mohammad Amini Dehaghani has told Iran International that he was tortured into making a false confession, denied effective legal representation and deprived of the chance to appeal his death sentence.

Qatar, Pakistan push Iran-US diplomacy as war escalates. Qatar and Pakistan have launched a joint effort to revive Iran-US diplomacy as military exchanges entered their ninth day, while Tehran confirmed receiving new mediation proposals even as hardliners continued to oppose negotiations.

Beyond espionage: Araghchi says spies seek to shape Iran's decisions. Foreign intelligence penetration of Iran is hardly a secret. But Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has now suggested the operation goes beyond locating officials or stealing information and seeks to influence decision-making inside the Islamic Republic itself.

France accuses Iran of assaulting diplomat, warns of consequences. France has accused Iranian security services of detaining two members of its embassy staff for several hours and physically assaulting one of them, in what Paris called a serious breach of diplomatic immunity that "cannot go without consequences."

Iran MP says government considering petrol price rise despite war and inflation. Iranian officials are discussing a possible increase in petrol prices, although no proposal has yet been formally presented to parliament, the spokesman for parliament’s Energy Committee said.

Araghchi interview draws fire from Iran hardliners. Criticism of Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's recent interview has spread across Iranian conservative media, with critics arguing he disclosed sensitive information about wartime security and internal decision-making following its publication this week.

Iran economists say war is turning malaise into crisis. Iran's leading economists warned Monday that renewed conflict with the United States risks pushing the country's long-festering economic problems into a more dangerous phase, arguing that inflation is becoming increasingly difficult to contain.

Iran secretly buried first of 12 sentenced to death in protest case. Iranian authorities secretly buried teenage protester Erfan Esfandiyari without his family present and have reinstated the death sentence of another young defendant in the same Isfahan case, sources told Iran International.

Two men sentenced to death for helping wounded protesters in Shiraz. A Revolutionary Court in Shiraz has sentenced political prisoners Mojtaba Dehbandi and Kianoush Hamzehei Kazerooni to death for helping protesters wounded during the January uprising, Iran Human Rights reported.

Paris weighs reducing embassy staff in Tehran, source says. France is reviewing whether to reduce staffing at its embassy after two French diplomats were detained, interrogated and allegedly abused by Iranian security forces in Tehran, according to information obtained by Iran International on Tuesday.

Hardliner accuses Ghalibaf of paving way for coup through US deal. A hardline Iranian lawmaker accused parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf of backing a US deal that blocks revenge for Ali Khamenei’s killing and could paralyze the state, paving the way for a bloodless coup.

Pakistan races to preserve Iran-US MoU amid widening war. Pakistan and Qatar are pressing ahead with efforts to revive Iran-US diplomacy, but Tehran has yet to publicly endorse the initiative as fighting continues over the Strait of Hormuz and resistance to renewed negotiations grows within sections of the Iranian establishment.

After Hormuz, are Iran-backed Houthis closing another vital strait?. Several tankers carrying Saudi crude oil reversed course on Tuesday after Tehran-backed Houthis declared a blockade on shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, raising fears that the US-Iran war could disrupt a second major energy chokepoint.

Bulgaria’s move to allow US aircraft draws NATO member closer to Iran war. Bulgaria moved Tuesday toward allowing US aerial refueling aircraft to support Middle East operations, drawing a warning from Tehran and raising the risk of the NATO member being pulled into the Iran-US conflict.

Why Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain has become Trump’s next target. President Donald Trump vowed Tuesday to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, but experts say the deeply buried nuclear facility, potentially central to Tehran’s efforts to restore enrichment, may be far harder to disable than his warning suggests.

Rubio says US will strike Iran shipping threats, remains open to diplomacy. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday that Iran was under severe economic and military pressure but the United States would continue targeting its ability to attack commercial shipping while remaining open to a negotiated solution.

Bombing Iran's coast misses the target in Tehran, analysts warn. The US may be peeling away layers of Iran's leadership, but without a plan for what comes next, bombing the coast and seizing islands cannot reach the problem in Tehran, and risk delivering an IRGC takeover rather than real change, experts said at an Iran International town hall.

Raid on Tehran's cafés was a show of contempt. The latest round of café closures in Tehran is a reminder to ordinary Iranians that wartime or otherwise, those in power still decide how much space they are allowed to occupy.

Rushdie attacker contacted person in Iran before attack, US prosecutors say. US federal prosecutors said the man convicted of stabbing author Salman Rushdie contacted a person in Iran before the 2022 attack to confirm that the fatwa calling for Rushdie's death remained valid, the New York Times reported, as his federal terrorism trial opened on Wednesday.

Iran protester handed down three death sentences, rights group says. A Tehran court has sentenced protester Ahad Shokouhian to death three times over his involvement in January demonstrations, the Hengaw Organization for Human Rights reported on Thursday.

Rubio says Trump’s Iran policy is ‘a head for an eye’. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump’s policy toward Iran was “a head for an eye,” warning Tehran it would pay a heavy price for attacks on Americans and US interests.

French foreign minister says diplomats detained in Iran have returned home. France warned Iran of consequences on Thursday after Iranian security officers detained two French diplomats in Tehran for nearly four hours and allegedly beat one of them, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said, adding the diplomats had already returned home.

Unpaid wages push Iranian workers to brink. Iranian workers who have gone months without pay may have only two months of financial resilience left without government intervention, a labor representative warned on Thursday, as wage arrears mount following conflict between the United States and the Islamic Republic.

Trump threat to hit Pickaxe renews calls in Iran for nuclear bomb, NPT exit. President Donald Trump’s threat to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear-linked facility has intensified hardline calls for Tehran to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and develop a nuclear weapon.

Russia’s gasoline imports add pressure to Iran’s strained fuel market. Russia’s turn to imported gasoline after Ukrainian attacks damaged its refineries is adding demand to a tight Asian fuel market, creating a potential new complication for Iran as it struggles to cover a daily shortfall of about 30 million liters.

Iran-US rhetoric shifts from ships to infrastructure. Recent statements by officials in Tehran and Washington illustrate how public rhetoric has shifted beyond military deterrence toward explicit threats against civilian and energy infrastructure across the Middle East.

Oil rally hardens Tehran's stance on US talks. The surge in oil prices appears to be hardening Tehran's resolve against renewed negotiations with Washington, giving ammunition to those who argue that a prolonged conflict puts more pressure on the United States than on Iran.

Trump raises the stakes as Iran talks stall and conflict widens. President Donald Trump moved closer on Thursday to expanding the US campaign against Iran, threatening both a major new military operation and financial punishment as diplomacy faltered.

Hormuz traffic falls to one as US-Iran fighting escalates. Just one vessel transited the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, the lowest daily traffic since May 7, as the United States and Iran escalated military and economic threats while commercial shipping continued to avoid one of the world's most important energy chokepoints.

Iran bears biggest economic cost of Hormuz closure. Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz appears to have dealt far greater damage to its own trade with China than to Beijing's commerce with the rest of the Persian Gulf, according to newly released Chinese customs data.

Cafés close, tolerance ends: Iran’s post-war shift on compulsory hijab. Several cafés in central Tehran have been shut down after authorities renewed pressure over compulsory hijab, days after senior clerics called for stricter enforcement and weeks after the government briefly tolerated looser dress code during wartime pro-establishment gatherings.

Germany limits Tehran embassy services as it urges citizens to leave Iran. Germany has scaled back operations at its embassy in Tehran while again urging its citizens to leave Iran, the German Foreign Ministry told Iran International on Friday.

Ali Khamenei was killed at meeting on protest crackdown - security-linked outlet. A meeting at Ali Khamenei's office where he was killed in February was focused on preparations to manage future protests as well as responding to what officials believed was an imminent US-Israeli attack, according to Noor News, a security-linked media outlet.

Trump's Iran escalation fuels Senate clash over war powers. President Donald Trump's hint at a larger military operation against Iran has intensified debate in Washington, with Republican allies rallying behind the president while Democrats accuse him of violating the Constitution and seek to curb his war powers.

Tehran braces for possible new phase of war. President Donald Trump’s increasingly explicit threats of a wider Iran war have fueled anxiety and speculation inside the country, as analysts and social media users debate whether the conflict is approaching a more destructive and unpredictable phase.

Trump weighs major Iran strikes as more regional states enter the war. US President Donald Trump said Washington was in talks with Iran and had not yet decided whether to launch major new strikes, even as fighting spread across the region and reports emerged that Bahrain and Kuwait had directly attacked Iranian military sites for the first time.

Pezeshkian camp slams state TV over Khamenei US talks edit. Iran’s government has publicly accused the state broadcaster of censoring President Pezeshkian’s remarks in which he said the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei privately ordered officials to negotiate with the United States despite publicly ruling out talks with Washington.

Nearly half of Iranian internet users angry over conflict outage, ISPA poll finds. Nearly half of Iranian internet users said they were angered by the country's recent internet shutdown during the conflict with the US, while most opposed unrestricted internet access for government officials, according to a survey commissioned by the communications ministry.

Iran uses migrant smuggling routes to place operatives in Britain - Telegraph. Iran is using migrant smuggling routes into Britain to move covert operatives into the country, the Telegraph reported on Saturday, citing unnamed Iranian officials, people smugglers and analysts.

Guinée : Siguiri, capitale du RPG, tourne lentement la page Alpha Condé. Dans l’historique bastion de l’ancien parti au pouvoir, au nord-est du pays, les fidèles d’Alpha Condé se font discrets depuis le coup d’État de 2021. Entre nostalgie et ralliements opportunistes au nouveau président Mamadi Doumbouya, le fief du parti dissous cherche ses repères. Reportage.

Mines : le Gabon a-t-il les moyens de ses ambitions de transformation locale ?. En signant un protocole d’accord avec Eramet, Libreville franchit une nouvelle étape vers la transformation locale de son manganèse. Mais, en dépit des signatures et des discours, la réalité économique risque de s’imposer aux autorités gabonaises.

Cameroun : Marafa Hamidou Yaya, ou l’emmuré du SED. Condamné pour « complicité de détournement d’argent public », l’ancien secrétaire général de la présidence est détenu depuis quatorze ans à la prison annexe du secrétariat d’État à la Défense (SED). Tandis que son « complice », Yves Michel Fotso, coule des jours tranquilles en France.

Gabon-France : les coulisses de la visite d’État d’Oligui Nguema à Paris, entre faste et compromis. En déroulant le tapis rouge au président gabonais, Emmanuel Macron remercie un allié fidèle. Parmi les sujets délicats, la transformation locale de manganèse produit par Eramet, objet d’un discret bras de fer.

La retraite hyperactive de Trevor Manuel, rock star sud-africaine de la finance. Retraité sur le papier, Trevor Manuel multiplie les chantiers. L’ex-ministre des Finances de l’Afrique du Sud planche sur la réforme de la dette souveraine et l’intégration industrielle du continent.

Au Burkina Faso, RSF accuse Ibrahim Traoré de posséder une « milice numérique » qui cible les journalistes. Dans une enquête publiée ce 23 juillet, Reporters sans frontières argue que les cyberactivistes des BIR-C, rattachés à la junte, « occupent le terrain numérique et s’attaquent aux voix dissidentes en toute impunité ».

L’opposant algérien Fethi Ghares à nouveau condamné à deux ans de détention pour « outrage ». Figure de la gauche algérienne qui avait émergé avant la présidentielle de 2019, l’ancien acteur a depuis été plusieurs fois emprisonné. Sa condamnation tombe alors que le président Tebboune vient d’assurer que chaque Algérien a le droit de critiquer et d’exprimer ses désaccords.

Cameroun : les milliards dormants des prêts au développement. Projets bloqués, fonds dormants, taux de décaissement au plus bas… Yaoundé accumule les contreperformances face à ses bailleurs publics comme privés, dont certains menacent d’annuler leurs prêts.

10 choses à savoir sur le Sénégalais Birame Diop, le nouveau président de la commission de la Cedeao. Le général sénégalais, qui entrera en fonction le 1er septembre, est un militaire spécialiste des questions de paix et de sécurité. Un choix stratégique pour le président, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, qui prend lui-même la présidence tournante de l’organisation.

Ould Errachid – El Khattat : qui remportera la bataille des législatives dans le Sahara ?. Pendant près de vingt ans, l’Istiqlal a régné presque sans partage sur la région. Mais le départ spectaculaire d’El Khattat Yanja pour le PAM pourrait bouleverser les équilibres.

« Malgré les discours, personne ne veut de cette monnaie » : l’eco face à ses contradictions. La Cedeao a réaffirmé sa volonté de lancer l’eco en 2027. Dans les faits, les obstacles sont tels que l’échéance est impossible à tenir. Explications.

Africa Corps ouvre un corridor inédit entre Lomé et Bamako pour livrer des blindés au Mali. Un convoi de blindés russes a emprunté pour la première fois la route entre Lomé et Bamako, en passant par le Burkina Faso. Africa Corps trouve ainsi une alternative au refus de la Guinée d’accueillir un cargo sous sanctions.

Pourquoi la future Bourse de Kinshasa parie sur les géants miniers. La RDC s’apprête à lancer sa première place financière, ciblant en priorité le secteur extractif. Une ambition souveraine portée par une conjoncture minière exceptionnelle mais fragilisée par des déficits de gouvernance.

Afrique du Sud-France : pourquoi le Conseil d’affaires voulu par Macron est au point mort. Lancé en marge du G20 de Johannesburg, en 2025, par Emmanuel Macron et Paul Mashatile, le Conseil d’affaires franco-sud-africain peine à décoller. En cause, des modifications de listes imposées par le vice-président, de profonds désaccords et un manque d’intérêt.

Neutralisation des FDLR en RDC : les discrètes manœuvres diplomatiques de Kinshasa. Alors que les opérations contre ce mouvement fondé par d’ex-génocidaires hutu patinent, les autorités congolaises défendent auprès de leurs partenaires un protocole d’accord sur la démobilisation du groupe. Celui-ci est considéré comme une menace existentielle par Kigali.

Cameroun : Edgar Alain Mebe Ngo’o, ou la disgrâce d’un sécurocrate. Il avait gravi tous les échelons du sérail camerounais : préfet, patron de la police, directeur du cabinet civil du chef de l’État, ministre délégué à la Défense… Edgar Alain Mebe Ngo’o se croyait intouchable. Mais, un jour, la machine à broyer qu’il faisait tourner depuis trente ans l’a broyé à son tour.

Comment le christianisme a survécu – et se transforme – au cœur du Maghreb musulman. Le christianisme fait peu parler de lui en Afrique du Nord, hormis les visites du pape ou, comme cela a été le cas tout récemment à Rabat avec l’archevêque López Romero, quand des scandales éclaboussent le clergé local. Discrète, la religion chrétienne y est pourtant implantée depuis des siècles, et les fidèles ont changé.

Resolute Mining se rue vers l’or ivoirien pour compenser l’instabilité malienne. Le groupe australien investit 500 millions de dollars dans la mine ivoirienne de Doropo. Un pari sur le nouvel eldorado aurifère d’Afrique de l’Ouest.

Tunisie : Ayachi Zammel et Wadie Jary graciés, Rached Ghannouchi toujours en prison, dans un état « critique ». Alors que la défense du chef du parti islamiste Ennahdha condamne l’absence de réaction des autorités face à la « grave détérioration de son état de santé », Ayachi Zammel, un ancien candidat à l’élection présidentielle, et Wadie Jary, l’ex-président de la fédération de football ont, eux, été graciés à l’occasion de la fête de la République.

Dangote lève 2,5 milliards de dollars et vise la première place mondiale. Avec 2,5 milliards de dollars levés auprès d’investisseurs privés, la raffinerie Dangote franchit un cap. Le groupe nigérian vise désormais une introduction en Bourse et ambitionne de devenir la plus grande raffinerie au monde d’ici à 2028.

Sahara occidental : quelle marge de manœuvre pour les négociateurs du Polisario ?. Alors que le processus politique sur le Sahara occidental amorcé en début d’année sous l’autorité de Washington semble dans l’impasse, la délégation du Polisario pose question. Quel est le pouvoir réel des trois diplomates chevronnés qui la composent, et que peuvent-ils vraiment négocier ?

Wamkele Mene (Zlecaf) : « Nous ne pourrons pas réaliser le potentiel de l’Afrique si nous restons fragmentés ». Sept ans après sa signature à Kigali, la Zlecaf affiche des avancées institutionnelles mais le commerce intra-africain plafonne à 15 %. Wamkele Mene, son secrétaire général, défend le bilan et trace les perspectives.

Burundi : pourquoi le blogueur congolais Benjamin Babunga est-il toujours en détention ?. Arrêté le 27 mai à Bujumbura, où il vit et travaille comme humanitaire, ce passionné d’histoire présent sur les réseaux sociaux est accusé de terrorisme et d’espionnage. Il a pu se défendre et espère être bientôt libéré.

Mali : l’ex-patron des renseignements condamné à quinze ans de prison. Le colonel-major Kassoum Goïta a été reconnu coupable, le 24 juillet par la Cour d’assises de Bamako, de « complot contre le gouvernement ». L’ancien chef des renseignements nie et a ouvertement accusé la junte de corruption.

« Cela pose un problème moral » : comment le dossier Petromin rebondit au Maroc. Au Maroc, le litige autour de Petromin Oils connaît un nouveau tournant judiciaire. La Cour de cassation a accepté le renvoi du dossier vers Fès, invoquant une suspicion légitime de partialité à Casablanca.

Crise au PDCI en Côte d’Ivoire : tout comprendre aux procédures judiciaires contre Tidjane Thiam. Convoqué en urgence à la veille d’un verdict judiciaire redouté, le bureau politique du PDCI a dû être annulé en catastrophe le 23 juillet, sur fond de lutte des clans. Tidjane Thiam peut-il être destitué de la présidence de son parti ?

Oligui Nguema à Paris, que sont devenues les grandes figures du développement, négociateurs du Polisario, les « déchus de la République » du Cameroun… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur la visite du président gabonais à Paris, présente la nouvelle équipe des négociateurs du Polisario au Sahara occidental, raconte comment l’or finance la guerre au Sahel, dresse les portraits de ceux que Paul Biya a écartés de sa route au Cameroun et relate ce que deviennent les bâtisseurs du développement africain après avoir quitté les responsabilités.

Présidentielle 2027 au Nigeria : Bola Tinubu face au piège sécuritaire de l’opposition. Enlèvements, rançons, pression américaine : la crise nigériane s’invite dans la course à la présidentielle de 2027. L’opposition entend faire payer à Bola Tinubu le coût de l’insécurité et met la pression jusqu’à Washington, courtisé par les deux camps.

Intagrist el Ansari : « Le récit national malien s’est construit sur une imposture historique ». Né dans les campements nomades de la région de Tombouctou, l’écrivain et réalisateur malien issu de la communauté touarègue signe son premier long-métrage : « Ressacs, une histoire touarègue ». Un film à la fois intime et politique sur l’identité touarègue, tourné sur dix ans, entre le Nord-Mali et la Mauritanie. Interview.

Maroc : comment Mostafa Terrab a transformé OCP en géant des engrais. En vingt ans, OCP est devenu l’un des principaux acteurs mondiaux des engrais phosphatés grâce à un changement de modèle industriel et à des investissements massifs. Bien que spectaculaire, cette transformation s’accompagne de multiples défis dans un environnement incertain.

En Algérie, le « scandale des moutons » de l’Aïd embarrasse le pouvoir. Afin d’enrayer la flambée des prix avant la « fête du sacrifice », plus de 1 million d’ovins ont été importés dans le pays. Mais cette opération d’envergure, voulue par le président Abdelmadjid Tebboune, se retrouve au cœur d’un vaste scandale judiciaire.

« Il faut empêcher qu’Ebola ne devienne une menace régionale et internationale ». Face aux coupes dans l’aide au développement et au risque d’une plus grande propagation du virus en République démocratique du Congo, un collectif de responsables politiques et du monde de l’entreprise rappelle, dans une tribune au « Monde », qu’aucune société ne peut durablement protéger sa santé en affaiblissant celle des autres.

Aux Seychelles, loin de l’image idyllique, les ravages d’une multi-addiction aux drogues dures. « L’Afrique sous emprise » (4/6). L’héroïne, mais aussi la méthamphétamine, la cocaïne et le fentanyl se déversent sur cet archipel de 120 000 habitants dans l’océan Indien. Face à la crise, l’Etat tente de réagir mais manque d’informations.

Tanger Med, le grand port industriel du Maroc rattrapé par les tensions entre la Chine et l’Europe. « La ruée sur les ports » (14/16). Conçu pour être le marchepied de l’industrialisation du Maroc, le port Tanger Med a rempli son objectif. Mais les investissements chinois dans le royaume, attirés par des conditions ultra-favorables et une position stratégique dans le détroit de Gibraltar, font craindre qu’il ne devienne aussi l’une des portes d’entrée de Pékin sur le marché européen.

Quels sont les enjeux de l’implantation de Starlink en Afrique ?. En l’espace de trois ans, le service d’Internet par satellite du milliardaire Elon Musk, a réussi à déployer ses services sur le continent africain malgré une forte défiance des différents gouvernements.

La cheffe des députés écologistes, Cyrielle Chatelain, saisit Sébastien Lecornu sur le cas d’un lanceur d’alerte centrafricain sur Wagner. Réfugié en France depuis 2024, Ephrem Yalike-Ngonzo a été à l’origine d’une enquête de Forbidden Stories qui a révélé des opérations de désinformation menées en Centrafrique par le groupe paramilitaire russe.

Mali : l’ONU exige une enquête sur les tortures et les meurtres après une attaque au nord du pays. Le Haut-Commissariat des Nations unies aux droits de l’homme a exigé jeudi une enquête indépendante après l’exécution de dizaines de militaires maliens qui s’étaient rendus, lors d’une attaque de séparatistes touaregs et de djihadistes, début juillet.

« Il sera difficile de me défaire du traumatisme que j’ai subi » : après une année sous la menace d’une expulsion, une Franco-Algérienne obtient l’annulation de son OQTF. En juin 2025, cette femme, naturalisée française en 1997, s’est vu notifier une obligation de quitter le territoire français. Depuis, elle a vécu dans la crainte d’être arrêtée, avant que la justice n’invalide la décision de la Préfecture de police de Paris.

« Où est-ce qu’on va comme ça ? » : en Tunisie, où les températures frôlent 50 °C, la canicule met le pays sous pression. Les secteurs de la santé et de l’agriculture sont mis à rude épreuve par les coupures d’électricité, et les incendies se multiplient.

En Tunisie, l’opposant Rached Ghannouchi, incarcéré, est dans un état « critique », selon ses avocats. La défense du chef du parti islamo-conservateur Ennahda, âgé de 85 ans, a alerté sur une « grave détérioration » de son état de santé, après avoir appris qu’il avait perdu connaissance en prison.

« Jos le joufflu », le baron néerlandais de la cocaïne devenu vice-roi de Sierra Leone. « L’Afrique sous emprise » (5/6). Condamné aux Pays-Bas à sept années de détention dans une affaire d’importation de 11 tonnes de cocaïne, Jos Leijdekkers, gendre du président sierra-léonais, organise son trafic en toute impunité depuis Freetown.

« La Tunisie n’est plus dans une transition démocratique bloquée, elle est entrée dans une transition autoritaire inachevée ». Cinq ans après l’arrivée au pouvoir du président Kaïs Saïed, l’Etat tunisien est fragilisé par la destruction du système issu de la révolution de 2011, conjuguée à l’absence d’un modèle alternatif durable, analyse le militant démocrate Kamel Jendoubi dans une tribune au « Monde ».

Les Etats-Unis sanctionnent l’armée soudanaise pour l’usage d’armes chimiques. La décision américaine intervient après le largage de barils de chlore en septembre 2024. Des faits étayés par des enquêtes du « New York Times » et de France 24, que l’armée soudanaise continue de nier.

En Angola, l’affaire des « espions russes », reflet du tournant pro-occidental du pays. Igor Ratchin et Lev Lakshtanov, arrêtés en août 2025, ont été reconnus coupables d’avoir attisé un mouvement de contestation sociale, mené des campagnes de désinformation et interféré dans l’élection présidentielle, prévue en 2027.

En Guinée, une mobilisation en ligne inédite après les viols de jeunes filles mineures. Why is Cair urging US Muslims to seek security from DHS? Submitted by Muneeza Rizvi on Fri, 06/26/2026 - 22:15 The grant push is only the latest in the civil rights group's decades of steering Muslims towards the institutions that surveil, entrap and deport them Police and officials brief the media after a shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego on 18 May 2026 (Carlos A Moreno/Getty Images via AFP) Off Applications for this year's round of security grants from the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) close on 24 July - and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair) is urging mosques, Islamic schools and Muslim nonprofits to apply before the deadline. Since May's mosque shooting in San Diego, which killed three people, Cair has aggressively pursued renewed Muslim community access to this source of government funding, presenting it as a means of protecting mosques from such violence. Cair has since also encouraged Muslims to build closer ties with the police - reviving a debate over policing that reflects a growing divide within the community, between those eager to collaborate with "law enforcement" and those who view it as an arm of an unjust social order. Cair has long walked an ambivalent line on this issue. As a self-described civil rights and advocacy nonprofit with nearly 30 chapters, it positions itself as Muslims' primary defence against "overly-broad" policing. Yet, at the same time, it has spent decades encouraging Muslims to "build bridges" with the very police agencies whose practices it claims to challenge. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Cair's encouragement suggests that Muslims and "law enforcement" are two groups separated by unfamiliarity or misunderstanding. However, the history between them is not one of insufficient contact. Muslims have come to know local and federal police agencies all too well through a history of hostile encounters: decades of FBI door knocks, entrapment cases, raids of Palestine encampments that local police have turned into prosecutions of Muslim students, harassment outside Zionist land sales and relentless attempts to conscript Muslims into disciplining their own communities. Though spread unevenly, suspicion towards "law enforcement" has long existed among Muslims in the United States. Such sentiments became more visible in 2020, during the nationwide demonstrations following the police murder of George Floyd. And they have only become more pronounced since Israel's genocidal war in Palestine. Indeed, when any meaningful resistance to US foreign policy is met with police violence , it becomes difficult to ignore the link between occupation abroad and state repression at home. Despite this growing political consciousness among Muslims, Cair remains committed to strengthening Muslim cooperation with "law enforcement". 'Best practices' In the aftermath of the shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego, numerous Cair branches disseminated the national office's "Best Practices for Mosque and Community Safety", a booklet aimed at leaders and everyday congregants. Its recommendations take as given that Muslims embracing "law enforcement" will protect mosques from violence and desecration. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Best practices listed in the document thus include informing local police of mosques' daily schedules, inviting police to mosques for meetings and offering police training in cultural competency. Recommendations also extend beyond local "law enforcement". The booklet stresses: "Attempt to establish liaison with state and federal agencies in the same manner as you did with the local police. Local police may be able to facilitate this effort." Cair's best practices appear less concerned with Muslim defence than with having Muslims project respectability It also reminds congregations unable to afford private inspections of their security protocols that police departments can offer such assessments, as can specialists from DHS. Most bizarre is the booklet's jumble of non-evidence-based suggestions for deterring anti-Muslim violence. For example, it urges mosques to "acknowledge good work by individual police officers" and other local officials through "complimentary letters, phone calls, tweets, social media postings, annual award events, and the like". It also recommends that mosque leaders "be personally acquainted and friendly with the officer who is regularly assigned to [the mosque's] area". Though presented as guidance on "safeguarding" Islamic institutions, Cair's best practices appear less concerned with Muslim defence than with having Muslims project respectability. "The government exploits the Muslim community's perceived desire to fit in," insisted Terry Albury , an FBI agent-turned-whistleblower. Albury, who served a prison sentence for leaking government documents, underscored that authorities are not kept at bay by Muslims presenting as model citizens. He emphasised: "[FBI] sources are often willing volunteers who offer their services to the FBI in return for a favour... There are, however, situations in which a member of the community is led to believe they are doing their civic duty. An agent will often carefully cultivate this relationship in such a fashion that the person never views him or herself as a source and is simply being a 'good Muslim'." Despite "law enforcement" capitalising on some Muslims' need to be viewed favourably, Cair's booklet implies that deference and gratitude towards police can help protect places of worship. Histories of Muslim criminalisation, however, have demonstrated the opposite - that welcoming police to the mosque funnels Muslims into government crosshairs . Many Muslims who keep their guard up around the FBI still regard the local precinct as something separate and safer. The architecture of US policing, however, does not honour that distinction. Follow Middle East Eye's live coverage of Israel's genocide in Gaza (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Through multi-agency partnerships such as Joint Terrorism Task Forces, created to streamline communication between local and federal agencies, a Pizza with a Cop event at the local mosque can easily become a venue for data collection and community mapping. For more than a decade after 9/11 , the New York Police Department's Demographics Unit did just that, mapping Muslim neighbourhoods and cataloguing mosques, restaurants and student associations in a surveillance programme run with CIA assistance. "The government uses community outreach and the pretext of liaison for intelligence gathering... I would know because I employed these tactics with the FBI in both the San Francisco Bay Area and Twin Cities of Minnesota for many years," Albury warned. Cair's "Best Practices" booklet is littered with advice that many civil rights advocates would find alarming. Similarly concerning are Cair's changing recommendations on DHS's Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP), an initiative administered by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema). A transaction Muslim access to the NSGP has been a major priority for Cair since the San Diego mosque shooting. Funds from the NSGP are to enhance the physical security of nonprofits deemed "at risk of terrorist attack". Thus, money obtained through the programme could help a mosque with deteriorating facilities appear more like a military installation or sports stadium, with leaky pipes concealed behind DHS-approved blast-resistant trash cans . As a DHS programme, the NSGP is not a neutral means of protecting religious minorities, but part of the War on Terror's environment of information-sharing, in which federal agencies, local authorities and, ideally, "community partners" work in tandem. Developing the infrastructure for such interactions has arguably been DHS's key purpose. Communities are being told that the "threat" in question is the Islamophobic attacker outside the mosque door, but the programme's own paperwork belies that messaging. In it, the mosque is not only the protected party but an object of suspicion. US: DHS reviews security funding to Muslim organisations, places of worship Read More » Mosques cannot apply to Fema directly: applications are routed through state homeland security agencies, which score and rank them. Each applicant must submit a site-specific vulnerability assessment - a documented map of the facility's weaknesses - alongside the names and addresses of its board members, whose resumes are "subject to approval". The application also requires a mission statement, which the state assesses to validate "the central purpose of the organization". Houses of worship fall under DHS's "ideology-based" category, wherein applicants must flag any "practices that may elevate the organization's risk" and substantiate threats against them "based on their ideology, beliefs, and/or mission". A mosque seeking cameras must first submit its beliefs for review - and its staff for citizenship checks. This year's funding notice states that grantees "should not include foreign nationals or noncitizens", and that any they employ must be vetted under a policy it calls "staff American, stay in America". Before any award, DHS checks applicant organisations against "U.S. intelligence community reporting". Integration with these agencies is among the programme's stated objectives, and applications score higher for it. The notice's own funding priorities include "community engagement efforts to foster trust and encourage threat reporting", coordination with the government's suspicious activity reporting system, and "information-sharing platforms between ICE [US Immigration and Customs Enforcement] and local agencies". Before releasing a single dollar, Fema asks whether a recipient's "work or mission involves supporting aliens". Consider, then, a mosque whose Friday sermons defend Palestine or criticise US policy. The application requires it to decide whether that advocacy counts among the "practices that may elevate the organization's risk" - and to substantiate the threats it faces "based on [its] ideology, beliefs, and/or mission". To document why it is threatened, it must first file its politics with the state. That file is then checked against intelligence community reporting for "derogatory information" - a term the notice never defines - by the same department that arrested Mahmoud Khalil on the theory that his Palestine advocacy harmed US foreign policy. Any award can be terminated whenever Fema decides it "no longer advances the national interest". A mosque that wants to keep its new cameras has every reason to censor its sermons. Not a gift DHS also houses Customs and Border Protection, along with ICE, whose agents have shot and killed immigrants during raids and traffic stops, and whose detention cells last year saw their highest death toll in two decades. Muslim institutions are being pressed into partnership with the agency overseeing it all. As the NSGP's own 2025 call for applications emphasises, DHS emerged from the consensus that failures in communication helped make the 9/11 attacks possible. A quarter-century later, this origin story continues to shape how DHS views Muslims: as either threats to monitor or sources of intelligence to exploit. Thus, as attorney and researcher Ahmed Shaikh writes : "The [grant] is not a gift; it is a transaction in which you trade your community's sovereignty for lighting fixtures and a security camera." Cair actually offers the NSGP an easy path to future community buy-in. It also sanitises the broader counter-terrorism apparatus of which the programme is a part In this light, recent complaints about Muslims' unequal access to the grant (some citing structural Islamophobia ) suggest either a naive assumption that the NSGP is an impartial tool or a cynical attempt by politicians and "community leaders" to appear as defenders of Muslim interests. Cair itself expressed hesitation about the grant programme in 2020, warning that it could "enlist civil society organisations in activity that should remain in the purview of law enforcement". However, the same Cair statement concludes: " new DHS provisions [emphasis added] produce a de facto quid pro quo that pits the security of vulnerable communities against cooperation with law enforcement". While the statement correctly recognises DHS's attempt to fuse Muslim institutions with policing agencies, it reduces the problem to specific caveats within the NSGP rather than the post-9/11 reasoning underpinning the programme itself. Cair's position has thus frequently oscillated , at times reacting to DHS's shifting grant language, at other times to the party in power, and ultimately, to the functional exclusion of Muslims from the grant in 2025. It is not surprising, then, to see public statements by Cair criticising the terms of the NSGP - namely, its prohibition on grantees boycotting Israel and its mandating of cooperation with ICE. But this performance of critique is precisely what makes reformist politics like Cair's so insidious. By confining its objections to particular provisions, Cair actually offers the NSGP an easy path to future community buy-in. It also sanitises the broader counter-terrorism apparatus of which the programme is a part. As recently as 2024, Cair disseminated sample NSGP applications for mosques to emulate. In the model application, the fictional "Unity Mosque" emphasises its dedication to "maintaining a strong relationship with state and local homeland security partners". It seems Cair knows what kinds of proposals DHS actually funds. This focus on becoming the state's partner follows in the footsteps of Zionist organisations that have long been the primary beneficiaries of the NSGP. In fact, it is not only Cair but also Jewish Federations of North America that have been leveraging recent deaths in San Diego for access to greater NSGP funding. Perhaps the endpoint of Cair's trajectory is to resemble a group like the notoriously Zionist Anti-Defamation League (ADL). Decades of close coordination between the ADL and FBI gradually eroded the line between the two groups. In this sense, the issue with the NSGP - as far as the Muslim community goes - is not a particular provision nor the administration in power but its fundamental purpose: dissolving the boundary between Muslim communities and the police. But Cair has yet to reject the NSGP as such - hence its recent call for Muslim institutions to submit applications for the programme's 2026 funding cycle. Police work Cair's contradictions stem from its double role: it presents itself both as lawyer (defender of Muslims) and politician ("good" Muslim). The first role demands an adversarial posture towards state power and its categories of criminality, such as extremism and terrorism. This, however, conflicts with the aims of Cair-the-politician, whose appeals to local, state and federal officials revolve around portraying Muslims as law-abiding Americans. It can be difficult to discern where Cair ends and the police begin This muddiness in mission has enabled many puzzling occurrences over the years: a retired police officer as a Cair banquet keynote speaker, a deputy sheriff moonlighting as a Cair director for nearly a decade, the same officer reappearing as a "mosque security expert" following the San Diego mosque shooting, and even the occasional Know-Your-Rights training presented with "law enforcement". Akin to a cat instructing mice how to avoid capture, a civil rights workshop involving police is fraught from the outset. Whether through joint programming or recommendations that mosques honour police officers, Cair uses its trusted position as a community advocate to launder the image of predatory institutions. Because such efforts typically fall within the purview of police departments themselves (Community Relations Units), Cair's activity exceeds simple "bridge-building". It is police work. There is no shortage of "bridges" joining Cair and law enforcement - so many, in fact, that it can be difficult to discern where Cair ends and the police begin. It is therefore misleading to imagine Cair as standing on one shore and the police on another, constructing a "bridge" in between. A more accurate picture would place both on the same side of a river, extending a single bridge towards everyday Muslims. Will we step across, or choose a different path? Today, the market hums with familiar rhythms. Traders haggle over prices. Customers inspect fruit they increasingly struggle to afford. Life appears ordinary. Yet beneath the routine, residents say something has shifted. Not because Tunisia 's economic crisis has eased. Nor because confidence in politics has returned. Instead, many point to an event more than 2,000km away: Israel's war on Gaza . For Wajdi, and several other Tunisians MEE spoke with, Gaza has become a powerful political flashpoint, deeply intersecting with domestic issues. It's become a measure of the gap between official rhetoric and political action, reopening conversations that had largely fallen silent since July 2021 when Saied suspended parliament, sacked the prime minister and granted himself prosecutorial powers, invoking a national emergency in a move rights groups and political opponents called a coup. At first, many in Sidi Bouzid welcomed Saied's power grab, hoping a strong presidency would break years of political paralysis. But as the economic hardship deepened, many Tunisians lost faith that politics could improve their lives. Election turnout plummeted, public debate faded and conversations increasingly centred on making ends meet. Fifteen years after sparking the revolution, Sidi Bouzid remains among one of Tunisia's poorest governorates. Investment has failed to materialise, unemployment remains stubbornly high and many young people see emigration, rather than reform, as their only path forward. With inflation turning everyday shopping into careful arithmetic, traders say customers who once bought fruit and vegetables in bulk now only purchase enough for a few days. "Everyone has become poorer," Wajdi said, watching shoppers move between the stalls. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Gaza shifts attention to home When Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza, demonstrations spread rapidly across Tunisia. Tens of thousands took to the streets in Tunis and other cities, while Sidi Bouzid once again saw residents gathering in public around a political cause. Palestinian flags appeared en masse and marches drew in crowds who had not joined demonstrations for years. Residents said the demonstrations became one of the few spaces where people once again felt able to express political opinions publicly after years of silence. But as the death toll in Gaza mounted, many began asking why Tunisia's support appeared to stop at speeches. 'The regime displays hyper-sensitivity towards any street mobilisation, even when protesters raise officially endorsed slogans like supporting Palestine' - Khalil Lahbibi, Tunisian activist While Saied repeatedly condemned Israel, residents said they saw little effort to translate that rhetoric into meaningful diplomatic action or regional leadership. "I don't think Tunisia has done anything meaningful," Oumaima, a 26-year-old housewife, told MEE. "We haven't seen serious diplomatic efforts or attempts to build an international coalition. Why wasn't Tunisia leading efforts at the international courts [such as the ICC] or working to bring African countries together around a common position?" Instead, she pointed to South Africa, whose case accusing Israel of genocide at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) won widespread support across much of the global south. "Other countries stepped forward while Tunisia, despite all its statements about supporting Palestine, stayed on the sidelines," she said. "I expected much more." Several residents echoed those frustrations, arguing that the government's response had been defined more by rhetoric than action. They questioned why Tunisia had not attempted to rally African governments around a common position or pursue legal avenues against Israel, while other states pushed the issue onto the international stage. At home, they said, the contradiction became even harder to ignore. 'Government's actions tell a different story' While officials continued to present Tunisia as an unwavering supporter of Palestine, authorities launched a crackdown on activists involved in pro-Palestinian mobilisation, including participants in the Global Sumud Flotilla campaign. The arrests fuelled accusations that the government was seeking to monopolise solidarity with Gaza, allowing support for Palestinians only when it took place within state-approved boundaries while treating independent activism as a political threat. Khalil Lahbibi, a Tunisian activist involved in the Global Sumud Flotilla campaign, said Saied was seeking to "strike down the very idea of independent collective action". "The regime displays hyper-sensitivity towards any street mobilisation, even when protesters raise officially endorsed slogans like supporting Palestine," he told MEE. Because young activists and civil society organisations possess the capacity to mobilise and influence opinion, the regime treats them as direct political threats and potential rivals." Mohammed, a 22-year-old unemployed high school graduate, asked why Tunisia had largely confined itself to condemning Israel without attempting to lead any meaningful campaigns. "The government says it supports Palestine, but its actions tell a different story," he said. "It has arrested activists - people who were trying to show solidarity with Palestinians. How can you claim to defend Palestine while criminalising those standing up for it? That's a betrayal of the cause." Mohammed said Saied's speeches condemning Israel now carried little weight without concrete political action. "If he was truly serious, he would have worked with Algeria, Libya and other African countries to find ways of stopping weapons from reaching Israel, whether by sea or by air," he said. "Instead, we've only heard words while Gaza continues to suffer." Whether the war in Gaza marks the beginning of a broader political awakening in Tunisia remains uncertain. Years of economic hardship, repression and political disappointment have left many residents wary of predicting another uprising. Few in Sidi Bouzid speak openly of repeating the events that began here in 2010. But they say the silence that settled over the city has been broken. "The people will no longer be silent," Mohammed said. "This government hasn’t done anything for Palestine or Muslim causes. They now either need to step aside or step up, because the people have had enough,” he said. "We will not back down." Lt Gen Aamer Raza promoted to 4-star rank, appointed first Commander National Strategic Command. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has announced that Lieutenant General Aamer Raza, the chief of general staff of the Pakistan Army, has been promoted to the rank of a four-star general and appointed Commander National Strategic Command (CNSC), the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said on Friday. According to the PMO, the premier congratulated the newly promoted general and wished him the best for “undertaking this important responsibility”. General Raza has previously been awarded the Hilal-i-Imtiaz (Military) and Sitara-i-Basalat (Star of Valour). The CNSC post was created under last year’s 27th Constitutional Amendment , which made significant changes to the military’s chain of command, to assume the nuclear manager role previously exercised by the Chai­rman Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee (CJCSC), a post which was abolished. The appointment, reappointment and extension of the CNSC are tied solely to the recommendation of the Chief of Defence Forces (CDF), a post that was also created under the amendment for a unified command structure across the armed forces. Under the changes, the appointment, reappointment or extension of the CNSC or the “exercise of discretion by the appointing authority in this regard, shall not be called into question before any court on any ground whatsoever”. Last year, Field Marshal Asim Munir, who also serves as the Chief of Army Staff, was appointed the country’s first CDF following the passage of the 27th Amendment.

Anthropic bets on cheaper AI with new model. Anthropic on Friday released Claude Opus 5, a new artificial intelligence model the company says approaches the performance of its most powerful system at half the price. The San Francisco-based startup, a chief rival to OpenAI, said the model tops industry benchmarks for coding and knowledge work while consuming fewer computing resources than earlier versions. The claim addressed the rising concerns of business customers who have baulked at the expense of running advanced AI systems. Claude competes with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, and customers pay based on the amount of work performed, measured in units called tokens. Opus 5 costs $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, half the price of Fable 5, Anthropic’s most expensive publicly available offering. The company said the new model performs close to Fable 5 across many tasks despite the lower cost. Cost has become a major issue after Anthropic and its archrival OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, both filed for stock market listings in June. Wall Street is scrutinising their business performance more closely than ever ahead of their market debuts. On cybersecurity, Anthropic said it deliberately avoided training Opus 5 on cyber tasks, and that the model remains behind Mythos 5 — its most capable and most tightly restricted system, available only to select partners — on both offensive cyber work and biological research capabilities that could be misused. Mythos is Anthropic’s most advanced series of AI models, and its strength at finding weaknesses in computer systems — and at turning those weaknesses into working attacks — has caused controversy and pushed the company to build tight guardrails around them. The company said Opus 5 finds software flaws about as well as Mythos 5 but lags far behind in turning those flaws into something that could be weaponised into an attack. Citing the reduced risk, Anthropic said its automated safety filters will intervene roughly 85 per cent less often on Opus 5 than on Fable 5, the Mythos-class model it released last month. Fable 5 and Mythos 5 were briefly pulled from public access in June after the US Commerce Department imposed export controls, which were lifted at the end of that month.

IHC registrar issues notice to Justice Babar Sattar, asks him to vacate Islamabad residence. ISLAMABAD: Following the cancellation of the official accommodation allotted to Peshawar High Court (PHC) Justice Babar Sattar in Islamabad, the IHC registrar on Friday issued him a notice directing him to vacate the residence within 30 days. On April 28, the Judicial Commission of Pakistan approved the transfer of Justice Sattar from the IHC to the PHC. Following his transfer, Justice Sattar had decided to continue residing in the federal capital during his tenure at the provincial high court instead of seeking a separate official residence in Peshawar. According to the notice issued by the IHC registrar, the Estate Office cancelled the allotment of the official residence on July 3. The notice stated that Justice Sattar had been transferred from the IHC to the PHC and, following the cancellation of the allotment, had been given one month to vacate the premises. It further clarified that the 30-day period would be calculated from July 3, the date on which the Estate Office cancelled the allotment. Accordingly, the judge was required to vacate his Islamabad residence by Aug 3. Sources said Justice Sattar had earlier conveyed to the IHC administration his intention to retain the accommodation in Islamabad. The issue of official accommodation for superior court judges has long remained contentious. In 2023, a judgment authored by Justice Sattar held that judges were entitled to official accommodation from the date of their appointment and throughout their service, with the entitlement flowing from the presidential order rather than the general accommodation rules applicable to federal government employees. Sources further said officials visited Justice Sattar’s Islamabad residence on Wednesday but left shortly afterwards because the judge was on judicial leave and was not present at the residence at the time.

Terrorist attack on joint police checkpost in KP’s Tank martyrs 15, including 14 security personnel: ISPR. A terrorist attack on a joint police checkpost in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Tank district martyred 15 people, including 14 security personnel, the military’s media wing said on Friday. Among those martyred are 12 soldiers, two policemen and a government official. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said in a statement that the attack took place early on Friday and was carried out by Fitna-al-Khawarij — a term used to designate members of the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. Elaborating on the incident, the military’s media wing said the attackers attempted to breach the checkpost’s perimeter, but their attempts were “swiftly and decisively foiled by the vigilant and resolute response of security forces.” The security personnel deployed at the checkpost displayed “unwavering courage and professional excellence” and engaged and eliminated 12 terrorists, the ISPR added. The statement added that the attackers then rammed an explosive-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall. “Due to [the] blast impact, infrastructure at [the] checkpost was seriously damaged; resultantly, 15 brave sons of [the] soil, including 12 military, two policemen and a government official ex forest department, rendered the ultimate sacrifice and embraced shahadat (martyrdom),” the statement read. ISPR added that a sanitisation operation was ongoing to track down any other terrorists in the area, vowing that under the “relentless counter-terrorism campaign under vision ‘Azm-i-Istehkam’ (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”. “These sacrifices of our brave soldiers further reinforce our unwavering commitment to safeguarding our nation at all costs,” ISPR said. Last week, security forces killed 24 terrorists in KP’s Bannu district and its adjoining areas in the last 24 hours, the military’s media affairs wing said in a statement. The statement by ISPR said that there had been a recent “surge” in terrorist activities against police and suicide bombings in Bannu. “Security forces have initiated extensive joint intelligence-based operations to hunt the perpetrators of these heinous attacks and their support infrastructure. “Accordingly, in the last 24 hours, following fierce fire exchanges in Bannu district and adjoining areas, 24 khawarij belonging to Indian proxy Fitna-al-khawarij have been sent to hell,” the statement said. In May, at least 15 police personnel were martyred after a suicide attack on the Fateh Khel police post in KP’s Bannu district. The terrorists launched their attack on the post by ramming a vehicle laden with explosives. KP has seen a rise in terrorist attacks over the past year. According to the Annual Security Report 2025 from the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), KP recorded a significant surge in violence last year as “fatalities rose from 1,620 in 2024 to 2,331 in 2025”. Due to a resurgence of militancy, especially in KP and Balochistan, where attacks often target security personnel and LEAs , the state has intensified counter-terrorism operations.

Another bid to mend US-Iran fences ‘with China’s blessing’. TEHRAN: Iranian-made ‘Zulfiqar’ missiles are displayed at Azadi Square. The development came as US missiles struck targets across Iran on Friday after President Donald Trump vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the Middle East war to a second major shipping chokepoint, the mouth of the Red Sea. According to Reuters , exploratory discussions for the fresh push towards talks took place during a visit by Iran’s Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni to Islamabad this week , his second within the last 10 days. Earlier this week, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels had declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia , which signed a mutual defence treaty with Pakistan last year. Beijing, which has consistently backed Pakistan’s mediation efforts, had dispatched its special envoy in March to lead a shuttle-diplomacy trip around the Middle East. In a statement, China’s foreign ministry said “China supports the mediation efforts made by Pakistan and other parties.” It added that China will continue to “play an active role in restoring peace and tranquility in the Middle East Gulf region as soon as possible.” Separately, Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani called on all parties to commit to dialogue and to implement the terms of the memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran. Trump also said that he would hold Iran accountable for any further attacks by Yemeni fighters, “and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves”. Iranian media cited the head of Iran’s top joint military command as saying Iran would kill a member of the US forces for every Iranian killed. On Friday, US missiles struck a Revolutionary Guards Navy headquarters in the Ziba Kenar area of the Caspian Sea province of Gilan, according to a security official in Gilan. Provincial authorities said US projectiles had also struck the port city of Bandar Anzali, according to the ILNA news agency. Four people were killed and five injured in a US attack on the Iranian city of Ahvaz, the state broadcaster IRIB said. Diplomatic contacts Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar held a meeting with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Ara­g­hchi, on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s Council of Foreign Ministers Meeting in Cholpon-Ata, Kyrgyzstan. In a statement, the Foreign Office said the two top diplomats reviewed the ongoing regional situation and bilateral ties. “DPM/FM expressed deep concern over recent regional tensions and underscored the importance of dialogue, restraint, de-escalation by all sides, and sustained diplomatic engagement to achieve lasting peace and stability,” the FO said in a post on X. “He emphasised the need to build on the understandings reached und­er the Islamabad MoU of June 2026.” “The two sides agreed to maintain close coordination and regular consultations on issues of mutual interest and reaffirmed their commitment to working together for regional peace, stability and shared prosperity,” the statement concluded. Separately, in his remarks at the SCO summit, Mr Dar said: “Pakistan firmly believes that dialogue, diplomacy and mutual respect provide the only sustainable way forward to resolve conflicts and achieve durable peace and security.” He added that this principle led to Pakistan hosting talks between the United States and Iran in Islamabad in April, “enabling first high-level direct diplomatic contact between the two sides after 47 years”. You are like a son to me.” “Political sparring among parties should continue. There can even be some sharp exchanges, and that’s perfectly healthy. But there should be no fighting or violence.” “We have come with a pledge that, God willing, we will change the destiny of Mirpur and all of Azad Kashmir,” he said, while asking successive governments in Pakistan and AJK what they had done for the region since his ouster. He said the PML-N’s manifesto accorded priority to education and healthcare, promising new schools, colleges and universities as well as hospitals equipped with CT scanners and MRI facilities so that residents would not have to travel to Pakistan for treatment. Nawaz also announced a gift of 10 ‘Hospitals on Wheels’ and as many electric green buses for Mirpur from the Punjab government. He also pledged to dualise the Kotli-Nakyal road, construct tunnels at Lohar Gali and Leepa Valley in Muzaffarabad division, re­­v­­ive the long-stalled motorway project linking Mans­ehra, Muzaffarabad and Mirpur along the Jhelum River, and seek the establishment of an international airport in Mirpur. Speaking after him, CM Maryam argued that AJK did not suffer from a lack of resources but from inadequate infrastructure, insu­fficient welfare program­mes and poor governance. She asked the audience who had built the Kohala-Muzaffarabad Road, the Murree-Kohala Road and cardiac hospitals, prompting chants of “Nawaz Sharif” from the crowd. The Punjab CM pledged that welfare schemes introduced by the PML-N government in Punjab would be extended to AJK immediately after the elections, saying voters should support the party if they wanted development. “The world will see a clean Azad Kashmir after the elections,” she said, urging people to “think carefully” before casting their ballots. PPP hits back The announcement of schemes for AJK, including the ‘gift’ of 10 e-buses, during the campaign did not go well with the PPP. PPP-Parliamentarians Secretary General Nayyar Bukhari strongly criticised the PML-N leadership for gifting 10 electric buses, bearing CM Maryam’s images, to AJK during the election campaign and described the move as “political bribery”. He demanded the chief election commissioner take immediate notice of the transfer of the buses. Some PPP candidates for AJK Assembly elections, including Sardar Javed Ayub, Sardar Mukhtar Abbasi and Syed Bazil Ali Naqvi, also opposed the PML-N move. Taking exception to Mr Sharif’s remarks about the PPP chief, AJK Legislative Assembly Spe­aker and PPP candidate Chaudhry Latif Akbar alleged a series of promises made by PML-N leaders during their election rallies constituted a violation of the election code of conduct, and called on the Election Commission to take strict notice. He told the presser the announcements amounted to an attempt to woo voters ahead of polls. Taking exception to Mr Sharif’s light-hearted remark at a Muzaffarabad rally that he would ask Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to make the PML-N’s nominee the next prime minister of AJK, Mr Akbar quipped: “Nawaz Sharif’s own brother did not make him prime minister, yet he comes here and complains about it.” Referring to Punjab CM Maryam Nawaz’s claims, Mr Akbar alleged the PML-N leadership was attempting to “buy Kashmiri votes” through pre-election promises. Separately, Sindh Information Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon hit back at Mr Sharif’s jibe, saying: “Do not make the land and people of Sindh and Kashmir a subject of ridicule and humour”. Political differences ha­­ve their place, but ridicule of any province, city or area is not acceptable un­­­der any circumstances, he said, terming the ex-PM’s remarks “not only frivolous but also ridiculous”. Following the changes, the price of petrol stands at Rs335.18 per litre, while that of HSD stands at Rs383.46 per litre. The government is charging a total of Rs110 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs96 on diesel. The Petroleum Division’s notification said the new prices would be applicable for July 25 (Saturday). The diesel price has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. The daily pricing decision was rejected by the All Pakistan Dealers Association, which said it would consider a protest plan this week. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

PM again urges Kabul to act against terrorist groups. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and CDF Field Marshal Asim Munir jointly inaugurate the Sky47 AI Cloud centre.—APP • Says interim Afghan govt has failed to prevent its territory from being used for attacks against Pakistan • Announces Rs300bn Karachi-Chaman dual carriageway, expansion of education, infrastructure and solar projects in Balochistan • Inaugurates Sky47 AI Cloud facility in federal capital ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Sheh­­baz Sharif on Friday again urg­ed Afghanistan to take action agai­nst terrorist organisations and ensu­­re that Afghan soil was not used for terrorist activities against Pakistan. “Pakistan shares over 2,600-kilometre border with its neighbour and has repeatedly urged the Afghan authorities to act against terrorist organisations and prevent Afghan territory from being used against Pakistan. However, the Afghan interim government has failed to take effective action against these groups,” the prime minister said while addressing the National Workshop on Balochistan. The prime minister reaffirmed the federal government’s commitment to providing all possible resources for the development and prosperity of Balochistan, saying Pakistan could only progress when all provinces advanced equally. He announced that the Rs300 billion dual carriageway project from Karachi to Chaman would be completed within two years. Punjab, he said, had contributed Rs150bn to Balochistan under the National Finance Commission (NFC) Award. He added that other provinces had to play their full role in supporting the Balochistan’s development. The premier said Balochistan had been granted an additional 10 per cent quota in the distribution of laptops and scholarships, and that the Kachhi Canal Project would be completed on a fast-track basis. He praised Balochistan’s contributions to Pakistan’s development and prosperity, saying its leadership had always placed the national interest above personal or political considerations and had wholeheartedly supported the federation. He noted that farmers in Baloch­istan had suffered prolonged power outages for years. To address this issue, around 27,000 agricultural tube wells were being converted to solar energy under a Rs75bn project, to which the federal government had contributed Rs50bn. He expressed deep sorrow over the martyrdom of Mastung Judge Abdul Hakeem Kakar and a security official, praying for the elevation of their ranks and for patience for their families. The prime minister alleged that India was financing terrorism inside Pakistan. He added that although terrorism had largely been eliminated by 2017-18, it later resurfaced through what he described as a highly organised conspiracy. AI cloud centre inaugurated Later, PM Shehbaz described the newly inaugurated AI and cloud computing facility as a landmark achievement for Pakistan, reflecting the country’s growing technological capabilities. Addressing the inauguration ceremony of the country’s first-ever Sky47 AI Cloud centre, the prime minister praised the engineers, experts and institutions involved in the project and said the successful execution of the facility showcased the extraordinary talent available in both Pakistan’s military and civilian sectors. Paying tribute to Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir’s leadership, he said the project stood as a testament to what could be achieved when state institutions worked together with a shared national purpose. The prime minister also acknowledged the contributions of Field Marshal Munir, the Ministry of Information Technology, the IT secretary and strategic technology partner ZTE for their roles in delivering the project. The inauguration ceremony was attended by Field Marshal Munir, federal ministers Shaza Fatima Khawaja and Attaullah Tarar, as well as senior government officials. Published in Dawn, July 25th, 2026

Iran calls for expanding strategic cooperation with Pakistan. ISLAMABAD: As efforts continue to prevent the conflict in the Gulf from widening, Iran on Friday called for expanding strategic cooperation with Pakistan, describing Islamabad’s diplomatic engagement as an important contribution to regional peace and stability. “Pakistan has played a constructive diplomatic role in facilitating negotiations and advancing efforts towards regional peace and stability,” Iran’s Ambassador to Pakistan Reza Amiri Moghadam said while delivering the keynote address at a roundtable discussion, organised by the Centre for International Strategic Studies. “Strengthening our bilateral cooperation is essential for addressing contemporary security challenges in West Asia,” he said. The discussion, titled Pakistan-Iran Relations and Strategic Stab­i­lity in West Asia, brought together diplomats, academics, defence analysts and researchers to examine the future trajectory of Pakistan-Iran relations against the backdrop of an increasingly volatile regional security environment. Opening the discussion, CISS Exec­utive Director Amb Ali Sarwar Naqvi said the recent escalation had generated fresh uncertainties for regional peace, maritime security and global energy markets, making sustained dialogue and regional engagement more important than ever. Former ambassador Masood Khan said Pakistan’s consistent advocacy of peaceful dispute resolution and its ability to maintain constructive relations with regional and international stakeholders had strengthened its credibility as a facilitator of dialogue, confidence-building measures and de-escalation. Director General of the Institute of Strategic Studies, Islamabad, Amb Moinul Haque said the resilience and national unity displayed by the Iranian people during the recent conflict had played an important role in enabling the country to confront the challenges arising from the crisis. Dr Nazish Mahmood of Quaid-i-Azam University said greater cooperation between Pakistan and Iran in border security, trade, energy and regional connectivity could contribute meaningfully to long-term regional stability. Discussing the maritime dimension of the crisis, retired Rear Admiral Faisal Shah highlighted the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz as one of the world’s principal energy chokepoints and cautioned that prolonged instability there could carry far-reaching consequences for international trade, energy security and maritime stability. Dr Bilal Zubair, director of research at CISS, said the recent conflict had brought Pakistan and Iran closer than ever before, with their shared border, economic interdependence and common concerns over regional instability reinforcing bilateral cooperation and reshaping the relationship across political, economic and strategic domains.
